Chapter 22

Dates, money and distances in a locale

Everything that is not interface text: dates and ranges through cached Intl formatters, a headless date range picker that speaks CalendarDate, a transport hook that carries one across the wire, amounts in and out of minor units, and distances in kilometres or miles.

By the end of this chapter

Format and parse locale-dependent values with Intl and @internationalized/date, and move a calendar date from a picker to the server without turning it into a string by accident.

The translated strings are a few hundred keys. The values around them — every date, every amount, every distance, every country name — are not strings anybody wrote; they are computed, and the locale changes the computation. This chapter is about the three places a value crosses from data to a person’s eyes and back.

Dates and ranges

Chapter 10 explained the cache and the UTC round trip. What it did not show is the result. formatDate("2026-05-10", "de", "day") is “Sa., 10.”; in English it is “Sat 10”; in Portuguese “sáb., 10”. formatRange for the tenth to the seventeenth gives “10 – 17 May 2026”, “10.–17. Mai 2026” and “10 – 17 de mai. de 2026”. Nobody wrote any of those; the DateFormatter from @internationalized/date is Intl.DateTimeFormat with a fix for a Safari bug, and it knows.

The trips page puts them together with the plural messages from the last chapter: a date range from Intl, three counts through Paraglide’s plural rules, and a distance through the library’s formatDistance. Four sources of locale-awareness in one paragraph, and the component knows about none of them.

A date range picker that speaks the domain’s type

Bits UI is headless: it renders the markup, the ARIA and the keyboard model of a date range picker — segmented inputs you can type into, arrow keys between segments, a calendar grid — and nothing visible. Its value is a pair of CalendarDates from @internationalized/date, the type chapter 10 chose for the domain, so there is no conversion to get wrong. The name on each input renders a hidden <input> with the ISO date, which is how the value reaches a remote form and how it would reach a plain HTML form with JavaScript off.

The locale prop is Paraglide’s current locale, so the segments come out in the locale’s order — month, day, year for English; day, month, year for German — and the weekday names in the calendar follow. untrack around the initial value says out loud that the props are the starting point and the picker owns the value from then on; without it, the compiler asks whether you meant to track the prop, and here the answer is no. Every visible pixel — the field’s border, the segments, the popover, the calendar — is in src/lib/styles/dates.css rather than the component’s <style>, because an expense’s single date (chapter 31) wears the same look through a sibling component, and a component’s CSS ships only with the pages that import it.

calendarLabel={label} names the calendar grid; without it Bits UI calls every calendar in the app “Event”, in English. The two dates sit in one datefield__dates group that may wrap, and the calendar button stays outside it: at 360px “mm/dd/yyyy – mm/dd/yyyy” and a 36px button are wider than a card’s column, and a field that cannot shrink pokes out of the card. And each segment is rendered through the child snippet, which is the part worth slowing down for.

Bits UI writes two English words into every segment, with no prop to change them: aria-label="day, " and, until something is typed, aria-valuetext="Empty". A German screen-reader user heard “day, Datum, Empty”. A headless library usually leaves a door for this, and here it is the child snippet — Bits computes the props, hands them over, and lets us render the element. segmentAttributes is spread *after* Bits’ props, so its values win: the part’s name from Intl.DisplayNames with type: 'dateTimeField', which is the browser’s own locale data (“Tag”, “mês”), “Empty” from the messages, a data-empty attribute so the stylesheet can grey a placeholder without matching an English word, and aria-invalid plus aria-describedby pointing at the issue line when the form has one — Bits only knows invalidity from its own validate, and nothing of the server’s. The calendar’s two month buttons had the same English, “Previous” and “Next”, written after any aria-label passed to them; the same child snippet renders each button with the page’s “Vorheriger Monat” after Bits’ props, so ours is the one that lands.

Why this matters

Why not patch the library, or post-process the DOM? A patch is a fork you maintain at every upgrade, and a script that rewrites attributes after render fights the library’s own updates. The child snippet is Bits’ documented extension point: when Bits renders those strings differently, or adds a prop for them, this function is the one place to change. Two tests hold it. date-segments.spec.ts pins the function — a German day is “Tag”, a typed value is left alone, the separators are untouched — fed a hand-written stand-in for Bits’ props, which by itself would pass forever: if a Bits release renamed “Empty”, the stub would still say “Empty”. So DateField.svelte.test.ts renders both fields in a real browser with Bits doing the computing, on a German and a Brazilian page, and asks the segments and the month buttons what they say (chapter 44).

A CalendarDate across the wire

Load results and remote function arguments cross the wire through devalue, which knows Map, Set, Date, typed arrays — and nothing about a class from @internationalized/date. The transport hook teaches it: encode returns something falsy for “not mine” and the ISO string for a CalendarDate; decode parses it back. With this, a value that leaves the browser as a CalendarDate arrives on the server as one, with .compare() and .add() working, rather than as a string somebody has to remember to parse. It is small; it is also the difference between a type that holds across the boundary and one that does not.

Money in and out

The amount field is type="number" with inputmode="decimal", so a phone shows a numeric keyboard with the locale’s decimal separator, the currency sits inside the field as a trailing adornment, so the number is what is typed and the unit is what is read, and the browser hands the form a plain number — which is why the remote form’s schema takes v.number() and the server converts to minor units with the trip’s currency. formatMoney on the way out uses Intl.NumberFormat with style: "currency": “€12.60”, “12,60 €”, “R$ 12,60”. parseAmount exists for the one place a free-text amount is typed, and it discovers the separators from Intl rather than knowing them — once per locale, then kept.

Distances, and a hundred country names for free

Two more Intl APIs. style: "unit" formats a kilometre or a mile with the right abbreviation and spacing for the locale; a unit the code has never seen still comes out right. Intl.DisplayNames with type: "region" turns PT into “Portugal” and JP into “Japan”, “Japan” or “Japão” — a hundred country names in three languages that nobody translated, from the browser’s own locale data. The gazetteer stores a two-letter code and nothing else.

Every Intl object here is built once and kept — a DateTimeFormat or NumberFormat loads locale data when it is built, and an itinerary formats forty dates a render. The shared helpers keep theirs in a module-level map: formatter() in dates.ts, formatMoney and the separators parseAmount discovers, and the library’s distanceFormat() above. A component that needs one builds it once, at the top of its script, as the explore page does with DisplayNames. The cache keys always include the locale. That sentence is the whole of project 5’s i18n bug, and it is why formatter() in dates.ts exists. The distance formatter was the last to join: the first version built a new NumberFormat on every call, and the trips list formats a distance per card on every render.

Checkpoint

  • You can say what formatRange does that two formatDate calls do not.
  • You can explain the transport hook’s encode/decode contract and what devalue does without it.
  • You can name the four Intl APIs this chapter uses and what each replaces.
